name: asdf (Mir/D)
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-element JSON array of mixed float/string/nested-object records (kostya/benchmarks 'Json' test) into a DOM and compute simple statistics, run in an identical Docker container on the same CPU as RapidJSON.
claimed_speedup: 0.133s (D/ldc2, Mir Asdf DOM) vs RapidJSON 0.154s (g++) and 0.194s (clang++) (~1.16x-1.46x faster, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: D/ldc2 1.41.0, LDC2_BUILD = -O5 -release -boundscheck=off; RapidJSON built gcc/g++ 16.1.0 and clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with COMMON_FLAGS = -O3 -march=native -flto=auto (kostya/benchmarks common/commands.mk)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian GNU/Linux (Docker image)
tradeoffs: D-only (needs ldc2/DUB toolchain, not usable from C++ directly); part of the larger Mir numerical ecosystem so pulls in extra dependencies; smaller community/less battle-tested than RapidJSON.
caveats: Single-run benchmark numbers (± shown, no repeated-trial stats besides the listed error bars); win margin over RapidJSON is modest (5-16%); result is specific to this one synthetic workload, not a general claim.
found_via: Starting query 'nativejson-benchmark json benchmark comparison winners' led to kostya/benchmarks as a maintained independent multi-language shootout; opened its README Json results table.

name: jsoniter-scala
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-element JSON array of mixed float/string/nested-object records (kostya/benchmarks 'Json' test) into an object model and compute simple statistics, on the same machine/container as the C++ entries.
claimed_speedup: 0.147s (Scala/jsoniter-scala) vs RapidJSON 0.154s (g++) and 0.194s (clang++) (~1.05x-1.32x faster, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Scala 3.8.4, sbt-assembly release jar; RapidJSON built gcc/g++ 16.1.0 and clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with COMMON_FLAGS = -O3 -march=native -flto=auto (kostya/benchmarks common/commands.mk)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian GNU/Linux (Docker image)
tradeoffs: JVM-only, needs code-generated codecs per-type at compile time (macro-based), not a drop-in DOM parser like RapidJSON; JVM warmup/startup cost not captured by this steady-state benchmark.
caveats: Win margin over RapidJSON(g++) is small (~5%); single synthetic workload; JVM long-run throughput can look better than short-lived-process use would.
found_via: Starting query 'nativejson-benchmark json benchmark comparison winners' led to kostya/benchmarks; opened its README Json results table.

name: zimdjson
workload: On-Demand-style parsing/field extraction over a 626MB systemsPopulated.json dump and twitter.json, measuring GB/s for tasks 'find-system', 'top-factions', 'coordinates', 'top-tweet', 'partial-tweets', run head-to-head against simdjson On-Demand/DOM and yyjson in the project's own benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: zimdjson (On-Demand) beats simdjson (On-Demand) on 3 of 5 tasks: ~1.5x on find-system (1.74 vs 1.18 GB/s), ~1.5x on top-factions (1.60 vs 1.04 GB/s), ~1.5x on coordinates (1.63 vs 1.06 GB/s); simdjson (On-Demand) is faster on top-tweet and partial-tweets (derived from page chart data)
compiler_and_flags: Zig, optimize mode selected via `zig build` (standardOptimizeOption); exact Zig version and optimization level used for the published charts not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Zig-only reimplementation of simdjson's On-Demand API (not usable from C++ directly); mixed results (loses on 2 of 5 published tasks); README itself cautions 'do not trust any benchmark, always verify it yourself'; author also notes zimdjson's unordered On-Demand mode is the slowest of all tested parsers on the schema benchmark.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own repo/author); numbers read off bar charts (images), not a table; no fixed compiler flags or Zig version recorded alongside the results; results are workload-dependent, not a uniform win.
found_via: WebSearch 'JSON parser benchmark 2025 faster than simdjson C++' surfaced discussion of simdjson ports/reimplementations; followed to EzequielRamis/zimdjson's Performance section.

name: jsonparser (buger)
workload: Schema-less field extraction from small (190B HTTP log), medium (2.4KB Clearbit-style), and large (24KB Discourse-API-style) JSON payloads, benchmarked with `go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5` against encoding/json, gjson, sonic, ffjson and easyjson.
claimed_speedup: Large payload: 20,114 ns/op vs encoding/json struct 130,565 ns/op = 6.5x faster, 0 B/op and 0 allocs/op vs 4,432 B/op and 147 allocs/op; small payload EachKey 227 ns/op vs 1,300 ns/op (~5.7x faster) (verbatim from page table)
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs; comparison libraries pinned to latest versions as of 2026-07-29
tradeoffs: No reflection/struct binding by default (path-based `Get`/`EachKey`/`EachObject` API instead of Unmarshal-into-struct), so migrating from encoding/json requires rewriting access code; returns []byte slices into the original buffer rather than copies unless told otherwise.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own repo) though methodology (hardware, Go version, run count) is fully stated, so treated as Tier A; numbers are Apple-silicon ARM64, not the x86 hardware most servers run.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'json parser faster than' surfaced 'New JSON parser for Go: up to 9x faster than encoding/json' (buger/jsonparser); opened repo README Benchmarks section.

name: gjson
workload: Same small/medium/large-payload path-lookup benchmark suite as buger/jsonparser (190B / 2.4KB / 24KB JSON records), run with `go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5` against encoding/json and four other Go JSON libraries.
claimed_speedup: Small payload: 402 ns/op vs encoding/json struct 1,300 ns/op (~3.2x faster); large payload: 22,756 ns/op vs 130,565 ns/op (~5.7x faster) (verbatim/derived from page table)
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5, Go 1.26.3, median of 5 runs; comparison libraries pinned to latest versions as of 2026-07-29
tradeoffs: Path-query API (`gjson.Get(json, "path.to.field")`) rather than struct unmarshalling; large-payload run allocates 28,672 B/op (not zero-allocation, unlike buger/jsonparser) because it builds result values on demand.
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party repo's (buger/jsonparser) benchmark suite rather than gjson's own, though methodology (hardware, Go version) is fully documented there; Apple-silicon ARM64 hardware.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'json parser faster than' -> buger/jsonparser README Benchmarks table, which lists gjson as a compared library beating encoding/json.

name: ujson4c
workload: Parse citm_catalog.json (1737KB, a large indented catalog file used in several JSON parser benchmarks) into a DOM (nativejson-benchmark 'Parse' test).
claimed_speedup: 1.841ms vs RapidJSON 1.950ms and RapidJSON_Insitu 1.922ms on citm_catalog.json (~1.04-1.06x faster, derived from page CSV data)
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 7.0, 64-bit, release configuration via premake5 (nativejson-benchmark build system)
tradeoffs: Wraps UltraJSON's C tokenizer with a decode-helper layer; RapidJSON is still faster on the other two test files in the same suite (canada.json, twitter.json), so this is not a general win; project has been archived since 2015 (unmaintained, GitHub-flagged 'Other' license though the bundled LICENSE.txt is a standard BSD-3-Clause EA grant).
caveats: 2016-era benchmark numbers on old hardware/compiler (clang 7.0); win margin is only ~4-6% and workload-specific (only wins on citm_catalog.json, loses on the other two files); repo archived and dead since 2015.
found_via: Starting query 'nativejson-benchmark json benchmark comparison winners' -> opened miloyip/nativejson-benchmark sample performance CSV and ranked per-file parse times.

name: sonnet
workload: Unmarshal canada.json-style geometry (canada_geometry, many floats) and citm_catalog.json into Go values, measured in MB/s, alongside encoding/json, sonic, goccy/go-json, json-iterator/go, easyjson, segmentio/encoding, valyala/fastjson and minio/simdjson-go.
claimed_speedup: canada_geometry unmarshal: 271 MB/s vs encoding/json 62 MB/s (~4.4x faster); citm_catalog unmarshal: 511 MB/s vs encoding/json 112 MB/s (~4.6x faster) (verbatim from page chart data)
tradeoffs: Reimplements JSON decoding from scratch (does not call encoding/json internally, unlike some 'fast' wrappers); on some workloads (e.g. canada_geometry) it is still slower than bytedance/sonic and minio/simdjson-go, so not the overall fastest.
caveats: Benchmark repo is maintained by the same author as sonnet, not a fully independent third party; no CPU model, Go version, or compiler flags are stated in the benchmark README, so methodology is incomplete; author's own README says the benchmark repo currently shows an old version of sonnet.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'json parser faster than' surfaced 'Show HN: Sonnet - The fastest JSON parser I can think of in Go'; followed link to the linked sugawarayuuta/benchmark results repo.

name: pikkr
workload: Extract 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 named fields (via JSONPath-like queries, e.g. $._id.$oid) from a 1GB generated JSON file (repeated 'companies.json' startup-company dataset) using AVX2-accelerated speculative parsing, compared against serde_json and the `json` crate.
claimed_speedup: 1 query: 954 MB/s (pikkr) vs 452 MB/s (serde_json) = ~2.1x faster; 16 queries: 816-966 MB/s (pikkr) vs 232 MB/s (serde_json) = ~3.5-4.2x faster (verbatim from benchmark repo output)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.22.0-nightly, cargo 0.23.0-nightly, release build (RUSTFLAGS default; requires AVX2), serde_json 1.0.3
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel Core i7 @ 3.3GHz, 2 cores, 16GB RAM
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose DOM parser: implements the Mison 'speculative parsing' algorithm which only extracts a fixed, known set of field paths from records with a stable/repetitive structure, falling back to slow-path parsing when the structure varies; requires Rust nightly and an AVX2 CPU.
caveats: Abandoned since 2017 (no commits in ~9 years); requires nightly Rust toolchain that may no longer build with current rustc; benchmark uses a purpose-built, structurally uniform dataset that favors pikkr's speculative-parsing design.
found_via: GitHub search 'topic:json-parser --sort stars' surfaced pikkr/pikkr; opened its Performance section and linked pikkr/rust-json-parser-benchmark repo for raw numbers.

name: DAW JSON Link
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-element JSON array of mixed float/string/nested-object records (kostya/benchmarks 'Json' test) into a schema-bound struct and compute simple statistics.
claimed_speedup: DAW JSON Link (clang++): 0.085s, NoCheck variant 0.070s, vs simdjson On-Demand 0.060-0.062s and simdjson DOM 0.103-0.107s, and vs RapidJSON 0.154-0.194s (~1.8-2.8x faster than RapidJSON; ~0.7-0.85x of simdjson On-Demand, i.e. slightly slower than On-Demand but faster than simdjson DOM) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 and clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with COMMON_FLAGS = -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (kostya/benchmarks common/commands.mk)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian GNU/Linux (Docker image)
tradeoffs: Requires describing the JSON schema at compile time via C++20 concepts/reflection-like macros (not a generic DOM parser like RapidJSON); the 'NoCheck' fast variant skips some structural validation, per kostya/benchmarks' own caveats and daw_json_link issue #226 on number-parsing inaccuracy.
caveats: Beats RapidJSON clearly but is slightly behind simdjson On-Demand specifically on this workload; single synthetic benchmark run; already on KNOWN_LIST, reported here only as new Tier A cross-language evidence per orchestrator note.
found_via: Starting query 'nativejson-benchmark json benchmark comparison winners' led to kostya/benchmarks; opened its README Json results table (independent multi-language shootout, not daw_json_link's own repo).

name: yyjson
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-element JSON array of mixed float/string/nested-object records (kostya/benchmarks 'Json' test) into a DOM and compute simple statistics.
claimed_speedup: 0.131s (gcc) / 0.132s (clang) vs RapidJSON 0.154s (g++) and 0.194s-0.262s (clang++, default vs Precise mode) (~1.17x-1.98x faster, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 and clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with COMMON_FLAGS = -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (kostya/benchmarks common/commands.mk)
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian GNU/Linux (Docker image)
tradeoffs: Pure C (no C++ needed) with both mutable and immutable DOM reader variants; slower than simdjson On-Demand and DAW JSON Link on this same table, so not an absolute leader, only beats RapidJSON specifically.
caveats: Already on KNOWN_LIST; reported here only as new Tier A cross-language evidence (independent, reproducible, compiler/flags/hardware all stated) per orchestrator note.
found_via: Starting query 'nativejson-benchmark json benchmark comparison winners' led to kostya/benchmarks; opened its README Json results table.
